dossier.public_summary: The dip looks flat and planet-sized, but its depth changes dramatically from one sector to the next and two of the seven transits are far deeper than the rest. A real planet must repeat at the same depth, so this is best explained by a few bad or spurious transits rather than a planet on the target star.

reasons.check: sectors depth change and per-transit scatter
reasons.why: Depth is not consistent across the light curve. Two of seven transits dominate the signal and are more than double the other transits, and per-sector depth increases by >130% within the same TESS-SPOC source (795 ppm in sector 9 vs 9077 ppm in sector 72). A real planet on the target must have the same undiluted depth; this transit-to-transit and sector-to-sector change is positive evidence for a few bad transits/false alarm, not a planet.
reasons.value: sectors p_constant 5.356e-7 depth_change_pct 134.9; transit_depths p_consistent 1.107903148555976e-19 share_of_top_3 0.969; transit depths 17049 ppm and 15632 ppm at 6.0 sigma and 5.4 sigma vs mean 6792 ppm

reasons.why: Flat-bottom shape and no odd/even difference or significant secondary alone do not prove a planet because a small-grazing stellar eclipse can also be flat and would show no secondary at this SNR. With the extreme depth variability above, the flat shape does not outweigh the evidence for systematics/contamination. Centroid is inconclusive and offers no on-target confirmation.

reasons.check: neighbour and density checks vs context
reasons.why: No star inside one TESS pixel can plausibly cause the dip with <=25% eclipse, and none as close as 3 sigma, so a directly blended NEB is disfavoured - consistent with a few outliers failing quality cuts or pipeline systematics on this faint Tmag 13.63 M dwarf. Size remains <=4.2 R_earth for all Gaia radii, and duration matches a central transit (fit_log_density_ratio 0.5866, b 0.1626), but this is insufficient when depth changes by an order of magnitude between epochs.
